t: Smallest Greater Multiple Made of Two Digits: Generate Candidates in Order
o: Among all positive integers whose decimal digits come only from digit1 or digit2, find the smallest one that is strictly greater than k and divisible by k, rejecting anything above 2^31 - 1. For k = 2 with digits {0, 2}, reading candidates in increasing order 2, 20, 22, ... the value 2 fails strictness and 20 is the first valid multiple. For k = 3 with digits {2, 4}, 22 is not a multiple of 3 but 24 is. With digits {0, 0} no candidate with a nonzero leading digit even exists, hence -1. Because at most two strings exist per length and lengths beyond 10 exceed the 32-bit range, exhaustively generating candidates in increasing order touches only about two thousand numbers.
k: Valid numbers are extremely sparse: fewer than 2046 values under 2^31 consist of a single repeated pair of digits.
Generating shortest-first and smaller-digit-first yields candidates in strictly increasing numeric order, so the first qualifying hit is the answer.
The multiple k itself must be rejected because strictness demands a value greater than k; every other multiple found is automatically larger.
Appending digits can overflow 32-bit intermediates, so compute in 64-bit and prune anything above 2^31 - 1.

a.i: Multiples of k arrive in increasing order automatically, so scan k, 2k, 3k and return the first one composed solely of allowed digits while also exceeding k. Digit tests cost O(log m) each. The weakness is density: when k is small the scan approaches two billion iterations and can exceed time limits, though it is trivially correct and fine for larger k.
s: Set m = k as the first multiple to consider.
While m does not exceed 2^31 - 1: check whether m > k.
If so, test every decimal digit of m against digit1/digit2.
Return m on the first full match; otherwise advance m by k.
Return -1 if the loop exits without a match.
a.t: O((2^31 / k) * log(2^31)) digit scans, up to roughly two billion iterations when k is small, which risks exceeding time limits.

a.n: Approach 2: BFS Generation in Increasing Order
a.i: Flip the direction: build candidate numbers from the two digits themselves, shortest first and smaller leading digits first, using a queue. Appending a digit preserves ordering across and within BFS levels, so pops occur in strictly increasing numeric order and the first qualifying candidate is minimal. Pruning anything above 2^31 - 1 caps the search at a couple thousand nodes regardless of k.
s: Deduplicate the two digits and sort them ascending.
Seed the queue with each distinct nonzero digit (no leading zeros allowed); an empty seed means answer -1.
Pop x: if x > k and x mod k == 0, return x immediately.
Otherwise push x * 10 + d for each sorted digit d, skipping values above 2^31 - 1.
a.t: O(C * L) where C is under 2046 generated candidates of at most 10 digits each, effectively constant work independent of k.
a.sp: O(C) for the queue of candidates.

w: Generate candidates in increasing order and stop at the first hit; be ready to explain why BFS layering plus ascending digits preserves numeric order. Pitfalls: accepting the multiple equal to k itself (strictness requires greater), overflowing 32-bit intermediates while appending digits, and forgetting that numbers like 0 or 00 are not valid since they carry no nonzero leading digit and never exceed k. Follow-up variants: allow a whole set of digits, change the modulus, or ask for the largest such multiple instead.
